o: Simulate a progressive tax schedule: dollars between successive bracket bounds ui−1 and ui are taxed at percenti, stopping once income is exhausted. Example 1: income 10 fills brackets (0–3 @50%), (3–7 @10%), (7–10 @25%) → 2.65. Since income ≤ 1000 and ≤ last upper bound, a simple linear scan works.
k: Track the previous bracket's upper bound; taxable amount in bracket i is min(income, ui) − prev.
Stop early once income ≤ ui; the guarantee income ≤ last upper means full coverage.

a.i: Accumulate tax bracket by bracket, clamping each slab at the remaining income.
s: For each (u, p): taxed = min(income, u) − prev; add taxed·p/100; prev = u; break when income ≤ u.
a.t: O(B) — one pass over at most 100 brackets.

a.i: Because income ≤ last upper bound, you can simply tax min(income, u) − prev for every bracket without an explicit break — the clamp makes later slabs contribute 0 once income is exhausted.
s: For each bracket add max(0, min(income, u) − prev) · p / 100 and update prev.
a.t: O(B) — single pass, branch-free per bracket.

w: Either version is fine; the clamped version avoids break-condition bugs. Pitfalls: taxing the whole bracket when income falls inside it, and integer division truncating percentages (use floating point). Edge cases: income = 0 and income exactly equal to a bound. Follow-up: marginal vs. effective rate computation.
